title: The mental map: what an AI Product Engineer actually needs to know
summary: This document presents an 'AI Product Engineer Roadmap' designed to transform individuals with basic tutorial experience into job-ready remote startup engineers within 3-4 months (10-20 hrs/week). It defines the AI Product Engineer as a practical role focused on shipping reliable LLM-powered products by contributing to real codebases, rather than theoretical research. The guide's methodology emphasizes shipping deliverables for each phase to foster learning. It outlines a 'mental map' of five core knowledge layers: LLM API fundamentals, context engineering (80% of the work), agents & orchestration, application engineering, and systems thinking, explicitly differentiating from research by skipping deep model internals. Phase 0 (Week 1) focuses on addressing foundational knowledge gaps for beginners.

title: Phase 0 (Week 1): Foundations you're probably missing
summary: This text outlines an AI Product Engineer roadmap designed to achieve job readiness in 3-4 months, focusing on building reliable products with LLMs by emphasizing practical skills and contributions to real open-source projects (Mastra, assistant-ui, mcp-use). It defines a 'mental map' of five core knowledge layers (LLM API fundamentals, context engineering, agents & orchestration, application engineering, systems thinking) while explicitly avoiding deep model research. Phase 0 (Week 1) covers foundational LLM concepts, API usage, and local dev setup, culminating in a dual-stack CLI tool. Phase 1 (Weeks 2-4) delves into comprehensive context engineering (RAG, chunking, embeddings, vector databases, hybrid search, evaluation), with a deliverable of building and debugging a RAG app. Phase 2 (Weeks 4-7) introduces agents, tool use, and MCP, linking to specific frameworks.

title: Phase 1 (Weeks 2–4): Context engineering — RAG done properly
summary: The text outlines a learning and development path for LLMs, starting with conceptual understanding (tokens, context, hallucination, attention) and API usage (Anthropic, OpenAI, including system prompts, streaming, tool calling, structured output, vision input). It recommends a local dev setup using Python and Node/TypeScript, followed by building a dual-language CLI tool with LLM API integration. Phase 1 focuses on Context Engineering/RAG, covering chunking, embeddings, vector databases, hybrid search, query transformation, evaluation, and RAG-vs-long-context tradeoffs, with a RAG-over-docs build project. Phase 2 introduces Agents, tool use, and MCP, linking to open-source frameworks.

title: Phase 2 (Weeks 4–7): Agents, tool use & MCP
summary: The text outlines a structured learning path for AI development, covering foundational LLM concepts, API usage, local development setup, and three progressive phases. It begins with conceptual LLM understanding (tokens, context windows, temperature, hallucination, attention) and major API features (system prompts, streaming, tool calling, structured output, vision input), alongside local dev setup using Python (venv, uv) and Node/TypeScript (pnpm, tsx, async/await). An initial build involves a dual-stack CLI tool with streaming LLM output and a single tool call. Phase 1 focuses on Context Engineering (RAG), detailing chunking strategies, embeddings, vector databases, hybrid search, re-ranking, query transformation, evaluation methods, and long-context vs. RAG tradeoffs, culminating in building and debugging a RAG app. Phase 2 covers Agents, Tool Use, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), including in-depth tool/function calling, agent loop patterns, MCP implementation, agent frameworks (Mastra, LangGraph, Vercel AI SDK), agent memory, multi-agent patterns, and computer-use agents. The build for this phase is a multi-tool agent wrapped as an MCP server. Phase 3 introduces Application Engineering, emphasizing the transition from demos to production-ready products.

title: Phase 3 (Weeks 7–10): Application engineering — making it a product
summary: The text outlines a comprehensive curriculum for AI engineering across four phases, covering agent fundamentals like tool calling (schema, parallel, error handling), agent loop patterns (ReAct, plan-and-execute, reflection), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It discusses agent frameworks (Mastra, LangGraph/LangChain, Vercel AI SDK), agent memory (short-term, long-term), multi-agent patterns, and conceptual differences in computer-use agents. The curriculum then moves into application engineering, including streaming UIs (server-sent events, optimistic updates), specific UI patterns (assistant-ui, Vercel AI SDK), structured output reliability (validation, retry, Zod/Pydantic), evaluation techniques (eval sets, LLM-as-judge), observability (tracing, token usage), guardrails (input/output filtering, prompt injection), auth/multi-tenancy, and deployment (containerization, secrets, rate limiting). Finally, it addresses systems thinking, cost/latency optimization (cost modeling, prompt caching, streaming-first UX, model routing), the decision between fine-tuning, prompting, and RAG, and AI-specific security basics. Each phase includes a practical 'Build' task, culminating in creating portfolio-ready projects and contributing to open-source initiatives.

title: Phase 4 (Weeks 10–14): Systems thinking, cost/latency, and portfolio polish
summary: The text outlines key aspects of developing AI applications, covering Streaming UIs (using tools like `assistant-ui` and Vercel AI SDK), ensuring Structured Output Reliability (via JSON schema validation and libraries like Zod/Pydantic), and implementing robust Evals (eval sets, LLM-as-judge). It also details Observability (LLM call tracing, cost/latency tracking), Guardrails (input validation, prompt injection), Auth, and Multi-tenancy. Deployment topics include containerization, secrets management, rate limiting, and queueing. Advanced concepts like Cost Modeling, Latency Optimization, Model Routing, and the decision-making between Fine-tuning, Prompting, and RAG are discussed, alongside AI-specific Security concerns. The text concludes by emphasizing the importance of turning projects into polished, deployed portfolio pieces incorporating an OSS strategy.

title: Weekly Learning Plan & Job Search Strategy for OSS Contributions
key_items: What to deliberately skip (research-track topics, not your job)
How this maps to your job search
summary: The document outlines a weekly learning schedule of 10-20 hours, divided into project building (40%), reading target open-source repository (OSS) code (30%) for job search, structured learning (20%) focusing on relevant resources while avoiding deep research papers, and writing up learned material (10%). It specifies research-track topics to intentionally skip, such as model pretraining/fine-tuning from scratch, distributed training, advanced transformer math, novel architecture research, and RLHF/RLAIF implementation details, emphasizing that only general understanding, not deep expertise, is required for interviews. The text then connects this strategy to the job search by linking specific target OSS repositories (Mastra, assistant-ui, mcp-use, Cua) to different learning phases and features. It sets an expectation for OSS contribution, aiming for small fixes by weeks 7-8 and shipping a real feature by weeks 10-14, which is a key component of the job outreach strategy.
